2. Third-Party Hearing Rights. As a general principle, third parties 
cannot demand hearings to determine someone else’s legal rights. There are, 
however, at least two situations in which a party who is not the subject of an 
agency’s adjudication may be able to force an agency to conduct an on-the- 
record proceeding.
First, hearing rights may be afforded to third parties who represent the 
pubhc interest that the agency is required to protect through a formal hearing 
process. For example. Office of Communication of the United Church of Christ 
V. FCC, 359 F.2d 994 (D.C. Cir. 1966), involved the license renewal application 
of a Mississippi television station. In reviewing a license application, the FCC 
is obhgated to determine whether the broadcaster is serving the public 
interest, convenience, and necessity.” 47 U.S.C. § 309(a). If the FCC is, for any 
reason * * * unable to make the [required] finding,” it is required to designate 
the hcense application for a hearing. 47 U.S.C. § 309(e). The petitioners, a local 
church and two civil rights activists, argued that the FCC was required to hold 
a formal hearing to give them an opportunity to present their allegations that 
the station, which was obhgated to broadcast multiple points of view on 
significant questions of pubhc pohcy, had refused to broadcast any 
programming in support of racial desegregation. The court agreed. This 
recognition of pubhc interest intervention rights accords with the idea that the 
representation of affected interests in admimstrative proceedings is key to the 
legitimacy of the modern administrative state. See Richard B. Stewart, The 
Reformation of American Administrative Law, 88 HARV. L. Re v . 1669 (1975).

one proceeding will compel its decision in a separate proceeding. For example,

separate requests before it: (1) Ashbacker had applied to change to a different
